I built GHZ states of 2, 3, 4 and 5 qubits. A GHZ state links all its qubits so they should always give the same answer, all 0 or all 1. I ran all four as one job of 4 circuits with 100 shots each. I tested it first on the free sirius:mock device (job 01a16053-849a-73bd-8e5d-d52a2bd767a3). The mock returned only all-zero results, so it proves the job runs but says nothing about quality. Then I ran one real job on sirius (job 01a16053-b198-76e0-b620-b1cf35d49762). The API reported 1.0 billed second, about 0.3 credits.

The fraction of shots where all bits agreed was 0.88 for 2 qubits, 0.86 for 3, 0.88 for 4 and 0.73 for 5. A perfect machine would give 1.0 every time. The trend is that agreement is lower on the real machine and drops most at 5 qubits. The 2, 3 and 4 qubit results are close to each other. With only 100 shots each, differences of a few percent between them are within statistical noise. The 5-qubit drop is larger than that noise would explain. The principle is that each extra qubit needs another two-qubit gate and another readout. Every gate and readout has a small error chance. These errors add up, so larger entangled states lose fidelity faster. This is why noise limits how big an entangled state can get on today's hardware.
